summary: A short note from Alex McKenzie at BBN that attaches network traffic statistics for the ARPANET for September 1972. The tables show how many packets each host sent over the period. BBN had been giving these figures to ARPA each month and now shared them with the whole network community.

eli5.summary: This is a monthly tally from the early internet, showing how many packets each computer sent. Think of counting how many letters each house mailed in a month, so the post office can see where the traffic is.

questions: how much traffic did each arpanet host send
subtitle: Monthly statistics on ARPANET packet traffic.

tldr.problem: BBN was collecting monthly ARPANET traffic statistics for the Department of Defense, but this operational data was not being shared with the network community.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 400 publishes the September 1972 traffic report, showing packet counts broken down by host and direction (inter-node and intra-node), for all 18 host sites active that month.
tldr.outcome: This was the first public release of ARPANET traffic data, and the practice of publishing monthly reports continued, providing visibility into network growth and usage patterns.

today: RFC 400 remains a historical snapshot of early ARPANET operations. The practice of publishing network statistics, initiated here, established transparency as a key principle of internet operations. Similar traffic reporting continues today through various network measurement and monitoring tools.

sections.title: The Traffic Report
sections.content:
RFC 400, authored by Alex McKenzie at BBN, publishes traffic statistics for September 1972. BBN operated the ARPANET IMPs and had been collecting these statistics monthly for the Department of Defense. This is the first RFC sharing this operational data with the network community, marking a shift toward transparency in network usage.

The report shows packet activity across the 18 host sites connected to the ARPANET at the time. Traffic is broken down into inter-node packets (sent to other hosts) and intra-node packets (sent to other hosts at the same site), allowing analysis of both network-wide communication patterns and local cluster activity.
sections.eli5: Someone from BBN wrote down how many packets went through each computer in one month, and shared the numbers so everyone could see what was happening on the network.

sections.title: Traffic Patterns
sections.content:
The September 1972 data shows significant variation in network usage. BBN's hosts handled the highest traffic, with Host 2 generating over 3.9 million inter-node packets and Host 3 handling 1.6 million intra-node packets—indicating heavy local and remote usage. MIT's hosts collectively sent over 1.4 million inter-node packets. UCLA, SRI, and other major computing centers also show substantial traffic.

The report includes average daily inter-node rates per host and a summary showing that across the month, the network carried about 24.8 million inter-node packets and 7.5 million intra-node packets. The average per-host-day was 27,478 inter-node packets and 8,386 intra-node packets. The ratio of packets to messages (1.07) indicates that most messages fit within a single packet.
sections.eli5: BBN was the busiest, but UCLA, SRI, MIT and others all sent millions of packets. The whole network together sent billions of packets in a month.

sections.title: Significance of Data Sharing
sections.content:
Publishing these statistics made the ARPANET community visible to itself. Network operators and researchers could see where traffic was concentrated, which sites were active, and how the network was growing. This transparency helped inform capacity planning, protocol development, and resource allocation decisions across the network.

These monthly reports became a standard part of ARPANET operations, with BBN continuing to publish traffic statistics. The data revealed the changing patterns of network usage as new services and protocols became available and more hosts joined the network.
sections.eli5: By sharing these numbers, everyone could see which computers were talking most and how busy the network was, helping them plan for the future.
